The mind creates the soul, the immaterial. So this is the good or the god; the good emanates and creates the shadow world in which we live. But our goal in life is to return to the good by seeking knowledge, learning truth, and mastering sacred geometry. Plato taught that secret geometry are shapes underlying reality. By mastering sacred geometry, one can master the fabric of the universe.

You want individuals to work hard to maximize energy for the empire, not just sit around reading books. Aristotle created a new philosophy counteracting Plato's ideas. For Aristotle, the material world is driven by cause and effect. This implies there must have been a prime mover—a first cause—ultimately attributed to God. However, only the end goal matters; we needn't concern ourselves with the beginning.

The end goal is telos or purpose, which means achieving one's purpose in life. Students should learn to become good students by fulfilling their purpose. Teachers aim to teach as well as possible. Work hard and produce energy for the empire. This conflict between Plato and Aristotle underlies Western philosophy; it emerges in Europe with rationalists like Descartes and empiricists.

Plato believes in mind over matter, while Aristotle emphasizes focusing on matter. The British Empire, along with all others, adopted this idea, including the American Empire. Greece's geography, being mountainous and hilly, made empire development challenging but fostered innovation among numerous conflicting city-states. Greece benefited from its proximity to the sea, allowing access to different parts of the world, including Persia, Egypt, northern Africa, Anatolia, Mesopotamia, and northern Europe.

The two major city-states were Sparta and Athens.
